newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Mixed emotions in HK on last day of British rule.
newsitem.headline: Mixed emotions in HK on last day of British rule.

text.p: With Chinese troops gathered on the border, Hong Kong residents on Monday started their last day under British colonial rule.

Stretching before them were a carnival day of pomp, pageantry and parties, along with a mixed undercurrent of emotions -- elation at returning to the Chinese motherland and concerns over future freedoms.
Dragon dances, the skirl of bagpipes, massive firework displays and marching bands were to be the order of the day.

In the Chinese capital Beijing, there was a festive mood. Streets were festooned with banners proclaiming "Wash away 100 years of national shame", and a blimp high over the city declared "Celebrate the return of Hong Kong".

Hong Kong becomes part of China on the stroke of midnight (1600 GMT) on Monday night, ending 156 years of rule that took it from a barely-populated rocky island to a teeming territory of 6.4 million that is one of the richest in the world.
Hailing Britain's achievements and welcoming the colony's return to China, the English-language Hong Kong Standard said the colony's economic future was as bright as ever.
"So Britain's departure is not the end of the world. It is no doomsday. It is not a time for tears. It is not goodbye Britain, welcome China," the newspaper said in an editorial.
Poised on Hong Kong's borders with China, troops of China's People's Liberation Army (PLA) were ready to enter the territory by land, sea and air in the hours around the handover.

The United States has joined Britain in sharply criticising the decision to send in 4,000 troops by armoured car, helicopter and warships. About 200 PLA soldiers have been in the colony for weeks carrying out logistics tasks for the arrival of the main force.
"I don't think this is the best way to start off," visiting U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said.

In the ceremony, Britain's heir to the throne Prince Charles hands over a 400 square mile (1,000 square km) area often described as a "Pearl of the Orient" to Chinese President Jiang Zemin. Britain's Union Jack comes down and the five-starred red flag of China rises.
Alongside China's flag will fly Hong Kong's own new flag, a local flower called bauhinia emblazoned on a red background.
British Prime Minister Tony Blair has his first meeting with Jiang shortly before the ceremony to chart a new course for Sino-British relations now that the Hong Kong issue is behind them.

On the eve of the handover, Jiang vowed to fulfil promises made by China under the 1984 Sino-British pact of "one country, two systems" that pledges to allow Hong Kong to carry on with its supercharged capitalist ways in the embrace of communist rule.

In another gesture of reassurance, Tung Chee-hwa, the shipping magnate chosen by Beijing to take charge of Hong Kong, for the first time on Sunday set a specific date of next May for elections to a new legislature.

A democratically-elected Legislative Council, Britain's parting political gift to Hong Kong and the focus of bitter Sino-British feuding, is being scrapped until the election in favour of a provisional legislature approved by Beijing.
Britain and the United States are sending only diplomats, not their main guests, to the legislature's swearing in shortly after midnight to protest that it was not elected.
British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook vowed to defend the democratic legacy. "It must be a prime objective of British policy to make sure that taste does not become a memory," he said.
Pro-democracy activists plan protests outside the Convention Centre where 4,000 VIPs will be on hand for the handover ceremony.
They have already erected huge banners outside the building.
One depicts the "goddess of liberty", symbol of Beijing's doomed 1989 Tiananmen Square democratic movement, crushed by Chinese troops with heavy loss of life.
Under controversial laws prepared by Tung's legislature, police approval will be needed for future demonstrations.
But with residents on five days of public holidays until Wednesday, the mood was relaxed.
Skyscrapers on either side of Hong Kong's spectacular Victoria Harbour were aglow with messages commemorating the transition.
Scores of parties and celebrations were planned to run alongside the official ceremonies.

Members of the famed Black Watch regiment and the last of London's other forces in Hong Kong hold one of the day's main events, a nostalgia-filled farewell parade at sunset, before leaving the territory shortly after midnight.
Prince Charles and Hong Kong's 28th and last governor Chris Patten leave at the same time aboard the royal yacht Britannia.
